THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. MAY 4, 1889. AFTER THE FLITTING. Bo 11. WHITHAM. It has 11....11 said that "three flits are as good as a fire." I tllll inclined to the opinion that too much moving about is quite as had as listing a rousing tire. Ile this as it may, we are now living in our third rouse--n flat since arriving in this city sixteen months ago. and I am glad to say we are much pleased vs ith it and its situation. We are situated within n hundred yards of the sea a bay I should say --and can enjoy- .' The rythmical Hoarse sounds that rise and fall Thuntrrons upon the ear from out at sea; The tumult nearer land. And splash upon the sand Of breaking waves compose one harmony." Entering at tire front door, steps to the number of twenty, carry us tip to the flat we call our house. A ball below, and a hall above, each some fifteens yards long, by about a yard antis half wide, come in quite handy as promenades. In England these halls would Inc called lobbies. but we in America ant much too democratic, and tilled with a thorough knowledge of our superior way of looking at t lunge, to descend to such ignoble terms. Proceeding on Uhrough the upper hall, we paits the kitchen ' door, and, looking out of the bark den, at once feast our eyes upon the splendid bay of San Francisco. I compare it in a modified way to look- ing over the sea from Uncle Tom's Cabin, at Black- pool, for our bay is a splendid sight on a nice morn- ing, with all its shipping Co near that we almost seem to be able tri ask tame of the English sailors how Salisbury likes Parnellism and Crime '— served up with Pigott I should say. all being well during the coming summer, I may 'winch out a little, and take up . with a few bad habits—l think Mr. N:dit or there is a pun somewhere in the iast line or two, and with my pipe and gluts stroll out on the verandah on moonlight evenings, and In tile late Matthew Arnold bids me Listen to the grating roar Of pebbles which tire waves straw back, and fling At their return up the high strand, Begin, and cease, and t hen again begin With tremendous cadence slow, Mal bring The eternal note of sadness in. Looking out to the left, and feeling determined not to see the dense black smoke wl.ich tire ill-devel- oped stack of the Pioneer Woollen Factory seems bent upon vomiting forth, we Pee the famous Golden Oates, the entrance to the bay. From this restless poina outward the Pacific ocean has its abiding place. Another s goak " inlr. Editor. lam afraid that a (eV: impediments stand in the way of my view, as with a glass strong enough I might take a look at you now and again, as with pick and spade you open out the Ship Canal. Yes, I am afraid t hat, the parallelua notwithstanding, a few difficult ie., standing in my way of being able toeven have a baik in at tire Toisn Ball while my friend Councillor Flood stirs his fellow Councillors up a little. But lam in hopes that science, all power- ful suit is, will have the telephone ready, so that I may listen to my friend Diggle, while lie expiates how the Ship Canal may be kept pure and undefiled by a stream whose rise shall be in the aromatic vales of Longfred. I think the above is somewhat mixed ; San Francisco and Warrington seem so muddled together in my liNal to-night that lean scarcely tell " from which ": I shall I aleep unit,
..... . . The above was written a fortnight ago, and dur- ing that time numerous letters and papers have reached as. the letters asking for information on . . _ .

every conceivable subject rdatingto California and San Prancisco in particular. The newspapers seem to be full of Pigottism ; the Tory paperaare espoially interesting. I quite enjoy the desperate efforts of the coercionist a in their struggle to get out of the quagmire the •• Times" has led them into. I have also received from Mr. Haynes a splendid picture of the .• G.0.M." Home Rulers in 'Warrington should not forget the public-spirited shoemaker in Ilorsemarket ; he deserves support. It is now the Ilest week in April, and what winter we have here is about over. Everyt ling is looking

really splendid. Roses of every hue ate to be seen in almost every garden. And the trills around, which a yearago, seemed barren, and unfruitful in every sense, .are now clothed in a beautiful vesture • has been of

of sjieen. 'file winter just past has lis4 one ... unprecedented wet ; rain has fallen in such copious quantities that the agricultural interest is jubilant enough to fill columns in the papere prophesying harvests of the roma bountiful description. CHARITY REWARDED IN AN UNDESIRABLE MANNER. Mary Heath, fifteen, a domestic servant, was brought before two county magistrates at Warring- ton, on Wednesday, on charges of having stolen a pair of bracelets valued at :is. 11.1., and also a silk handkerchief and scarf val Ilea at Ms., the pmperty of her employer, Mts. Pet ford, who is the occupier of the Red Lion Inn, Riston. The prosecutrix took the girl into her service out of charity, and clothed her. On the 901 of April the prisoner was suspec- ted of taking money out of the till, and upon her pockets being searched :14. od. was found. The girl afterwards decamped, hiving with her the articles mentioned. Prosecutrix stated that when she engaged the girl the latter refused to take money, and in n.turn for her services said she would rather be clothed, as her mother would only drink the money. The magistrates expressed a desire to deal leniently with the prisoner, and liberated her, at the same time binding her to appear when called 99. n.

A railway porter, named William Johnson, who has been employed on the Cheshire Lines, was pro- seemed at the Warrington Police Court on Thursday ' by his wife, who complained of a specific assault, and of the bad conduct other husband from a period 'shortly after their marriage. Mr. Jenkins. who appeared for the young woman, said that the parties were married at Padgate Church about four months ago, and prisoner commenced to ill-treat his wife about a fortnight afterwards. On the Pikh tilt, the date mentiOned in the charge, he nearly throttled ter, and struck her violently with Ids list. Ho also threated to kill her with a knife. She now asked for a separation order. Charles Edward Cunniagham, a lad of eight years of ages, has been getting into trouble. Ile appeared before the Warrington magistrates on Thursday, on a charge of theft, and li:stetted to the recital of his wrongdoing with stolid indifference. The boy, whose pansnts live in Blue Coat-st, was charged with having stole a coat, belonging to Michael Clausery, from a hut at the Dallam-forge siding. After the coat was mived, and tile matter inquired into, it was discovenssl that Cunningham haslgiven another lad three half-pence for pawning the coat for him. He then went to a Coffee Rouse, and purchased a bottle of eider and a scone. Whilst he was eating and drinking he made it known that he had come from Manchester, and, as he was on his way to Bolton. he would like a wash and brush. The people who keep the souse qiiestioned him, and at last he admitted that lie lived in Mile Coat-at. On Monday a married woman named O'Connor applied to the Warrington magistrates for a warrant against her husband, alleging that he had violently assaultEsl her. As hOth her eyes were discoloun,l, and her face had been otherwise injured, it was ordered that a free warrant should iota°, and it was made out on the spot. The husband, who is a eribinet-maker, was placed under arrest, and on Tuesday he was brought lip for trial. According to the statement of the complainant her husband quarrelled with her in regard to some household matter on Saturday, and, getting into a passion, gave her a violent blow between the eyes. The defendant in extenuation of his offsorirf., allege,! that his wife had "an angry tongue: lie was sent to prison for a month with hard laboar. Thomas Dutton, who is a farmer at Newtortsb ys Dareshary, Was charged at Daresbnry Sessions on Tuosday, with having worked a horse whilst in an entit state on the 27th April. P.C. Jackson of Preston liniok, said toe horse was being worked with sores on its shoulders and other parts of its hotly and legs. Defendant did not deny the charge and as he had before been summoned for cruelty to some horse he WAS tined 201. and costs. Defendant asin,d the Bench if he could have any protection from P.C. Jackson's insolence? The Chairman said if then, was any complaint to lie made against toe officer lie was sure the Chief Constable would attend to it. Defendant thought the officer treated him i very hardly. Chief Constable Ilamersley, who was in court, said if Mr. Dutton had any complaint to make lie should attend to it. AN EXCITINII Arena IN WINWICK-Rodn.

t Sarah Massey, wife of a wheelwright who lives at 277 Winwick-rd, attended at the Warrington County Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, to support a charge of assault against Elizabeth Burton, also a married woman, who lives in the same neighbourhom I. The ; complainant, who had Si,,' assistance of Mr. Arthur , Browne, bore marks of ill-usage on her face. The defendant was not legally represented, but her alt • tad,, literally breathed out defiance, and it could be . seen that she meant making a vigorous defence. On ' the solicitor's table a blood-stained handkerchief I and a parcel of hair were displayed as trophies of ; the affair to be inquired into. When the defendant had entered the dock, Mr. Browne incidentally ' remarked that "there wan a fearful smell of beer," ' and then proceeded to detail how,on the 28ral of April, the defendant went to Mrs. Massey's house to accuse the hitter of misconduct with her (defend ant's) husband, and used horrible and disgusting- language. Mrs. Massey closed the door, and there- upon Mrs. Burton smashed one of the panels with a piece of brick, broke into the house, gave Mrs. Massey a black eye, and scratched her face. Stir then threw a teapot through the window, and it hit an old woman on the arm, causingthe arm to bleed. The complainant bore out this statement in evidence, and called her hic.hand to speak as to the damage that had been none to the door. The defen- dant then had her turn, She alleged that complain- ant " insulted her most brutally," struck her, and threatened to kill her. A neighbour named Ann Jon., who was called for the defence, said that Whelk the two women were struggling on the Boor Mrs. Massey struck the defendant and threatened to " cleave her through the middle with a hatchet." The panel of the door had been cracked for a long hne. " That little woman," (the zomPlahmtd) watt like a tiger; she would " bite, and pinch, and scratch." Another neighbour spoke in corrobora- tion of the hatchet incident, and at this point the : magistrates. having evidently heard enough of the matter, dismissed the ease, and expiessed the ! opinion that one party was as had as the other.

div.p: BURNLEY GiZETTE, February 23rti. 1"7"AlIE lot of those who toil from day to, day in the bowels of the earth is not a very agreeable one. Apart from the terrible risks of which we an' so often reminded by a calamitous explosion, , .it'A•• - with all its thrilling scenes, the collier has to pursue his work at 'clines under circumstances of great hardship. Mr. Moses Knowles, of 109, Oxford Road, Burnley, has had some experlenee of the trying c:!.laiitions of labour in some of the deeper coal mines of this country. He relates bow lie has repeatedly had to work for hours crouched in ten or twelve inches of water and the cold liquid at the same time dropping all over his body from above. Happily such conditions 14. employment are almost unknown in the Burnley district, but Mr. Knowles has had to wicounter them in other mining :,:11•;•:,r in emisequence. He first commenced with pains in his %chid' gradually extended to other parts of the body. " I :;0 low," said Mr. Knowles, " that I was obliged to be covered :di blankets and have a chair v. It was only then that I could feel anything like warmth. My legs got so weak thct I H•cl to have the help of a stick to get across the floor. I was terribly troubled with indiges- nervous debility, and disease of the liver and kidneys, and had constant attacks of cramp in the stomach. For many weeks I suffered dreadfully, writhing in agony for hours together, ',I got so weak that it was painful to speak, let alone trying to move. ?Medicine only seemed to make me worse, and I got so that ray friends gave me up and the doctor ventured to offer no hope of a cure. At last I read one of 'Warner's pamphlets, sent for a bottle of 'Warner's SAFE Cure,' and oh ! how much good it did me. In a few weeks I was a new man. My appetite returned, the weakness disappeared, and I went back to my work feeling stronger them lt I had done lOr
